opus-5.5.text:
I think "changing the world" is a wonderful outcome, but I'm not sure it's a good *objective* for doing research day to day. When you set out with the goal of changing the world, it's very easy for the work to become about scale, about speed, about being the first to plant a flag. You start optimizing for impact metrics, for attention, for whatever looks like it will matter in six months. And sometimes that pushes you toward things you don't actually understand very well. You get a system that works, but you can't really say why.

For me, the more durable motivation is curiosity: wanting to know why something works, what the underlying principle is. In computer vision and in deep learning more broadly, a lot of progress has come from people who just couldn't stop asking simple questions. Why does this architecture generalize? What is the representation actually learning? Is this design choice essential, or just an accident of history? When you answer those kinds of questions carefully, the understanding tends to accumulate. Other people can build on it. It outlives the specific model or benchmark.

And honestly, I think understanding is often the path to changing the world anyway, just not a direct one. Many things that ended up being transformative started as someone trying to understand a phenomenon, not trying to build a product. If you chase impact directly, you're competing with everyone else chasing the same visible target. If you chase understanding, you sometimes end up somewhere nobody else was looking.

There's also a personal side. Research is a long game, with a lot of failure. If your only reward is changing the world, most days you'll feel like you're failing, because most days the world doesn't change. But if your reward is "today I understand something slightly better than yesterday," that's something you can actually feel. It keeps you honest and it keeps you going.

So it's not that I don't care about impact. I just think understanding is the more honest compass, and impact is something that follows from it, if you're lucky and patient.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to what you actually have control over.

"Changing the world" is an outcome. It depends on timing, on who picks up your work, on a hundred things outside the lab. If you make that the goal, you end up optimizing for impact signals rather than for whether something is true. You chase the benchmark, you chase the headline, and the day a paper doesn't land you feel like you failed, even if you learned something real.

Understanding is a process, and the process is something I actually own. When I ask "why does this work," or "what happens if I strip this away," I can answer that question today, in my own experiments, whether or not anyone cares. That makes research sustainable. It's a loop I can run every day, and the payoff is intrinsic.

And honestly, in my experience the two aren't in conflict. A lot of the work I've been part of that people say "changed the field" started as a very naive question. With ConvNeXt it was basically, is the Transformer really better, or did we just stop training ConvNets properly? That's not an ambitious question. It's a curious one. But the answer ended up mattering to a lot of people. Same with the self-supervised work: we weren't trying to build a product, we were trying to understand what representations emerge without labels.

So my view is that understanding is the cause, and changing the world, if it happens, is a side effect. If you aim at the side effect directly, you tend to miss both. If you aim at understanding, you at least get one, and sometimes you get both.

There's also a humility piece. The field moves so fast now that if you think you can predict what will matter in five years, you're probably fooling yourself. What survives is the clarity. A clean insight gets reused long after the specific model is obsolete.

astra-6.text:
For me, increasing understanding is a more concrete way to think about research. “Changing the world” is a powerful ambition, but it doesn’t tell you what question to ask tomorrow, or how to judge whether you’ve learned something meaningful.

When you do research, you’re working with uncertainty. You have an intuition, you run an experiment, and sometimes the result contradicts what you believed. If your goal is understanding, that contradiction is valuable. It can be progress even when your original idea fails.

I don’t think understanding and impact are opposed. Better understanding can eventually enable important changes. But that connection is difficult to predict, and I’m hesitant to make the eventual impact the justification for every research decision. I’d rather start with a question that matters, investigate it honestly, and try to leave us knowing something we didn’t know before.

sol-6.1.text:
I think changing the world is a wonderful ambition, but it’s very hard to use as a guide for everyday research. You don’t know in advance which idea will matter, or how it will be used. Understanding gives me something more concrete to work toward: can we explain why something works, identify which assumptions matter, and come away with a clearer question?

That doesn’t mean the research has to be disconnected from practical impact. Understanding can help us build better things. But if I judge every project by whether it will change the world, I’m tempted to overstate what I know. I’d rather make a contribution that clarifies something and let its impact grow from there.
